name: [Voyager] Notification consumer lag above 1000 messages
message:
{{#is_alert}}Partition {{partition.name}} of `voyager.notifications.outbound` is {{value}} messages behind for consumer group `voyager-notifications-v1`. Bookings are confirming normally and confirmation emails are not being sent.{{/is_alert}}
{{#is_warning}}Partition {{partition.name}} of `voyager.notifications.outbound` is {{value}} messages behind, past the {{warn_threshold}} warning line.{{/is_warning}}

**Why this is worse than it looks.** Nothing upstream is broken. The booking succeeded, the guest saw a confirmation page, the record is correct — and the email never arrives. This is the failure mode people only discover through support tickets, which is exactly why it is worth a monitor.

**Distinguish stopped from slow.** Open *Voyager — Data Layer* → *Consumer lag by group and topic*:
- **Straight line climbing at a constant rate** → the consumer is not consuming at all. It is paused, crashed, or stuck in a rebalance.
- **Climbing then flattening then climbing** → the consumer is running but slower than the producer. Throughput problem, not an availability one.

Then read *End-to-end notification lag (seconds)* next to it. Offset lag tells you how many messages are queued; the seconds tell you how stale the newest delivered message is, and that second number is what a guest actually experiences.

**Check the dead-letter queue too.** If *Notifications sent vs dead-lettered per minute* shows dead letters climbing alongside the lag, two things are wrong at once: the consumer is behind *and* the messages it does process are failing. *Dead-letter reasons by template* separates a failing email provider from malformed messages.

**Chaos flags that produce this.**
- `kafka_consumer_pause=voyager-notifications-v1` stops the group outright — this is the straight-line case. Reverse with `scripts/chaos.sh set kafka_consumer_pause ""`.
- `kafka_slow_consumer_ms=2000` adds per-message delay — this is the slow case.
- `kafka_poison_rate` and `email_failure_rate` fill the DLQ without necessarily creating lag.

All four together are scenario **S5**. Reverse with `scripts/chaos.sh revert S5`, or `make chaos-reset` for everything.

**Use Data Streams Monitoring for the full picture.** It reports lag from the client side as well, and a broker that is healthy while a consumer is stalled looks identical to a healthy system if you only have one of the three views.
{{#is_recovery}}Consumer lag on partition {{partition.name}} is back under 1000. The backlog will drain faster than it built, so expect a burst of delayed emails.{{/is_recovery}}
